summary.text: A previously healthy 10-year-old girl presented in April 2022 with abrupt neuropsychiatric symptoms: visual hallucinations, severe irritability, disorientation, dysgraphia, affective instability, obsessive-compulsive behaviors, catatonic/cataplexy-like episodes, social withdrawal and academic decline. A recent viral respiratory infection and lip herpes were reported by caregivers.

Risperidone 1 mg/day for 6 months at an external facility was ineffective; she was referred to the child psychiatry clinic and risperidone was discontinued after first evaluation because of elevated prolactin and poor clinical response.

Diagnostic workup included broad laboratory screening and pelvic/abdominal ultrasonography described as unremarkable, with only herpes simplex virus 1 IgG elevated; initial neurological examination and imaging at the referring center were non-focal. Repeat cranial MRI in the clinic showed bilateral hippocampal T2-FLAIR hyperintensities, and CSF showed low-titer NMDAR antibody positivity (1:100), confirming anti-NMDAR encephalitis.

Treatment comprised five-day courses of IVMP and IVIG, three additional cycles and rituximab for partial immunotherapy response, with valproate and olanzapine for psychiatric symptoms; sertraline was added and olanzapine was replaced by aripiprazole for side effects such as elevated weight and sedation.

By the 18th month of conventional treatment aggression, affect regulation and psychosis had substantially improved, and repeat MRI at the 24th month showed decreased bilateral hippocampal signal intensity, but persistent cognitive and executive deficits remained, documented by BRIEF-P and WISC-R scores.

With psychiatric stabilization and no further autoimmune relapses, memantine was started at 10 mg/day and titrated to 20 mg/day. At the 6th month she showed improved verbal output, reduced obsessions, better sustained attention and academic performance, lower BRIEF-P scores and higher WISC-R full-scale, verbal and performance IQ scores; mild nausea and hyperactivity resolved spontaneously, and psychiatric follow-up continues. Conventional first- and second-line therapies continued alongside memantine. The authors state causality cannot be established.
